definition:
The Bible teaches that God takes up the cause of people who have no one else to take it up: the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner living among his people. He does not merely pity them. He defends them, provides for them, and holds those with power to account for how they are treated. And he requires his people to do the same, not as an optional kindness but as part of what it means to know him. The law of Moses built this care into Israel's farming, lending, courts, and festivals; the prophets condemned Israel and Judah for crushing the weak while keeping up their worship; and Jesus began his public ministry by announcing “good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). The New Testament churches carried the same concern into their common life, collecting food for widows and money for the famine-struck believers of Judea. This study traces that thread. God's judgment on evil in general has its own study (Judgment and Justice), as does the right use of money (Money and Possessions).

The Hebrew vocabulary is rich. Mishpat means justice in the sense of a right ruling or the right ordering of things, including the rights owed to the weak; tsedaqah, ‘righteousness’, is faithfulness to the demands of a relationship. The two are often paired, and together they describe a society in which the vulnerable are not left to the strong. Several words name the poor. ʿAni means the afflicted or oppressed poor, a person bowed down by circumstances or by others; the related ʿanaw often leans toward the humble. ʾEbyon is the needy person who lacks what life requires; dal is the weak or thin, a small farmer with little margin; rash, common in Proverbs, is simply the poor person. The ‘fatherless’ (yatom) is a child without a father to protect and provide, whether or not the mother lives, and the widow (ʾalmanah) is a woman without a husband's household to secure her place. The ger is the resident foreigner, an outsider who has settled among Israel without land or clan, and he is repeatedly grouped with the widow and orphan. In the Greek New Testament the usual word for the poor is ptōchos, a person with nothing, often a beggar, as distinct from penēs, one who works for a living but has little, which appears only once (2 Corinthians 9:9). The stranger is xenos, the resident alien paroikos, and the widow chēra. None of these words is merely spiritual in the Bible's use, though Psalms and Isaiah also use the poor as a name for the faithful who depend on God alone.
ot:
The thread begins with a cry. When Cain kills Abel, God tells him, “The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10), and the question Cain throws back, “Am I my brother's keeper?” (Genesis 4:9), stands over the rest of Scripture. The exodus turns that cry into Israel's founding story. Israel was an enslaved foreign people in Egypt, and “their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God” (Exodus 2:23). God says, “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors” (Exodus 3:7). Everything the law later commands about the poor and the stranger rests on this memory. Other ancient law codes also spoke of protecting the weak; the epilogue of Hammurabi's laws (Babylon, about 1750 BC) presents the king as guarding the widow and orphan from the strong. What stands out in Israel's law is its motive: “You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Exodus 22:21), and “Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (Deuteronomy 24:18). Israel was to treat the outsider as God had treated Israel.

The law made that care concrete. Farmers were not to harvest to the edges of their fields or gather what fell; “Leave them for the poor and the foreigner. I am the LORD your God” (Leviticus 19:10). A forgotten sheaf was left in the field “for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow” (Deuteronomy 24:19). Every third year a tenth of the harvest was stored in the towns so that the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow “may come and eat and be satisfied” (Deuteronomy 14:29). Loans to a poor Israelite carried no interest (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36-37), a cloak taken as security was returned at sunset because “his cloak is the only covering he has for his body” (Exodus 22:27), and a hired worker was paid the same day “because he is poor and depends on them” (Deuteronomy 24:15). In the seventh year the land lay fallow “so that the poor among your people may eat from the field” (Exodus 23:11) and debts between Israelites were released (Deuteronomy 15:1-2). The Year of Jubilee, every fiftieth year, returned family land to the clans that had lost it (Leviticus 25:10), because “the land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine” (Leviticus 25:23). Whether Israel ever fully kept the Jubilee is uncertain, and the Bible records no instance of it; but its purpose is plain: no family was to be locked out of the land for good. Deuteronomy 15 holds together a hope and a realism. There should be “no poor among you” if Israel obeys (Deuteronomy 15:4), yet “there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). The courts were to be impartial in both directions: “you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich” (Leviticus 19:15). And the foreigner was to be loved, not merely tolerated: “love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34). God's own character grounds it all: “He executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing” (Deuteronomy 10:18).

The story of Ruth shows the law at work. A Moabite widow gleans in the field of Boaz, who goes beyond the letter of the law and leaves extra grain for her, and the foreign widow becomes the great-grandmother of David. The wisdom books teach the same thing as a matter of character. Job defends his integrity by saying, “I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper” and “I was a father to the needy, and I took up the case of the stranger” (Job 29:12, 16), and he grounds his duty to his own servants in creation: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them?” (Job 31:15). Proverbs turns this into theology in a single line: “Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him” (Proverbs 14:31). The king's task is to “defend the cause of the poor and needy” (Proverbs 31:9), and Psalm 72 prays that Israel's king will deliver the afflicted, “for their blood is precious in his sight” (Psalm 72:14). The Psalms call God “a father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows” (Psalm 68:5) and say that “the LORD protects foreigners; He sustains the fatherless and the widow” (Psalm 146:9).

The prophets bring the charge. Amos, preaching in the prosperous northern kingdom under Jeroboam II around 760 BC, condemns Israel because “they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals” (Amos 2:6), and he mocks the merchants who wait impatiently for the Sabbath to end so they can “cheat with dishonest scales” (Amos 8:5). Isaiah says Jerusalem's rulers “do not defend the fatherless” (Isaiah 1:23) and pronounces woe on “those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees” (Isaiah 10:1), showing that injustice can be written into law. Micah asks what God requires and answers, “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). Isaiah 58 tells worshipers that the fast God wants is “to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home” (Isaiah 58:7). Jeremiah warns that the temple will not protect a people who “oppress the foreigner and the fatherless and the widow” (Jeremiah 7:6), and he says of King Josiah, “He took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him. Is this not what it means to know Me?” (Jeremiah 22:16). Ezekiel names Sodom's sin as arrogance and complacency: “they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). After the exile the same issue returned. Nehemiah confronted Jewish nobles who were taking their poorer neighbors' fields and children as security for debts (Nehemiah 5:1-13), and Zechariah and Malachi repeat the old demand to protect the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the laborer (Zechariah 7:10; Malachi 3:5). The prophets also look ahead to a Spirit-anointed figure sent “to preach good news to the poor” and “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Isaiah 61:1), language that echoes the Jubilee.
nt:
The Gospels open on this note. Mary's song praises the God who “has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1:53), and Jesus himself was born to a family that could offer only the poor family's sacrifice of birds (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8) and was soon a refugee in Egypt (Matthew 2:13-15). John the Baptist tells the crowds, “Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none” (Luke 3:11), and tells tax collectors and soldiers to stop extorting. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and applies it to himself: “He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed” (Luke 4:18). When John's disciples ask whether he is the one to come, Jesus points to his works, ending with “the good news is preached to the poor” (Luke 7:22). In Luke the first beatitude reads, “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20), matched by a woe on the rich; in Matthew, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3). The two forms are not rivals. Matthew draws out the dependence on God that the Psalms already associate with the poor, and Luke keeps the social reality in view, so that neither the literal poor nor the spiritually humble can be dropped from the promise.

Jesus' teaching and practice press the point. He tells the host of a banquet to invite “the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” who cannot repay (Luke 14:13). In the parable of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:29-37), a lawyer asks, “And who is my neighbor?” hoping to limit his duty, and Jesus answers with a story in which the despised foreigner is the one who shows mercy, turning the question from ‘whom must I love’ to ‘to whom will I be a neighbor’. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) warns that a man who stepped past a starving beggar at his own gate every day faced God's reversal after death. Jesus condemns scribes who “defraud widows of their houses” (Mark 12:40) and in the next scene honors a poor widow's two coins (Mark 12:41-44). He calls justice, mercy, and faithfulness “the weightier matters of the law” (Matthew 23:23). And in the judgment of the nations the King says, “I was a stranger and you took Me in” and “whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me” (Matthew 25:35, 40). Interpreters differ on whether ‘the least of these brothers’ means any person in need or, more narrowly, Jesus' disciples in their need (compare Matthew 10:40-42); both readings make care for the needy a matter of how one receives Christ himself. When Jesus said, “The poor you will always have with you” (Matthew 26:11), he was echoing Deuteronomy 15:11, whose point was the duty to open one's hand, not permission to close it.

The church put this into practice from its first days. The believers in Jerusalem “shared with anyone who was in need” (Acts 2:45), so that “there were no needy ones among them” (Acts 4:34), a clear echo of Deuteronomy 15:4. When Greek-speaking widows were overlooked in the daily food distribution, the apostles did not dismiss the complaint; they appointed seven men to set it right (Acts 6:1-6). The church at Antioch sent famine relief to Judea (Acts 11:29), and when Paul's gospel was recognized by the Jerusalem leaders, “they only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). Paul spent years gathering a collection from Gentile churches for the poor believers of Jerusalem (Romans 15:26; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4; 2 Corinthians 8 and 9), grounding it in the incarnation: “though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). He describes its goal as “equality”, citing the manna in the wilderness (2 Corinthians 8:13-15). Converted thieves are to work so as to have “something to share with the one in need” (Ephesians 4:28). The duty reaches beyond the church, “let us do good to everyone”, while giving the household of faith a particular claim (Galatians 6:10).

James gives the sharpest statement. “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27). He rebukes a congregation that gave the rich visitor the best seat and told the poor man to stand, reminding them that God has “chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith” (James 2:5), and he warns landowners that “the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you” (James 5:4), the cry of Abel's blood and Israel's slavery heard once more. John asks how the love of God can abide in anyone who “sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him” (1 John 3:17). Hebrews calls believers to show hospitality to strangers and to remember prisoners “as if you were bound with them” (Hebrews 13:3), and Peter addresses the whole church as “foreigners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11), people who should know the stranger's life from inside. The Bible ends where the Psalms pointed. In the new creation the redeemed will never again hunger or thirst, and “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4).

keyTexts.why: The covenant code forbids oppressing the foreigner, the widow, and the orphan, forbids interest on loans to the poor, and says God will hear their cry because he is compassionate.
Gleaning law: the edges and leftovers of the harvest belong to the poor and the foreigner. Care for the weak is built into the ordinary work of farming.
The Year of Jubilee returns family land to those who lost it, because the land belongs to God. It became the Bible's great image of release.
God executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner, so Israel must love the foreigner, remembering its own years in Egypt.
Debt release every seventh year, with a command not to harden the heart. It holds together the hope of no poor and the realism that the poor will always need an open hand.
Job's oath of innocence treats care for servants, widows, orphans, and the naked as matters he will answer for before God, because the same God made them all.
To oppress the poor is to insult their Maker; kindness to the needy honors God. Care for the poor is grounded in creation.
God rejects fasting that ignores the oppressed and defines true devotion as freeing the yoked, feeding the hungry, and housing the homeless.
A king who builds his palace on unpaid labor is condemned; one who defended the poor is said to have known God.
Amos condemns those who trample the poor and take bribes at the city gate, and calls Israel to establish justice in the courts.
Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and claims it as the program of his own ministry: good news to the poor and release for the oppressed.
The parable of the good Samaritan answers a question meant to limit duty by showing a despised foreigner as the true neighbor.
The King identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick, and the prisoner, so that care for them is care for him.
Paul grounds the collection for Jerusalem's poor in Christ's becoming poor, and describes its aim as equality, with the manna as the pattern.
Favoritism toward the rich dishonors the poor God has chosen, and faith that sends a hungry brother away with words alone is dead.

history:
The early church became known for its care of the poor. Justin Martyr, writing his First Apology in Rome around 155, describes Sunday gatherings in which those who were able gave what they wished, and the gifts were kept by the presiding minister to help orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners, and strangers (chapter 67). In 362 the emperor Julian, who was trying to revive the old pagan religion, wrote to a pagan high priest in Galatia, Arsacius, complaining that the Christians supported not only their own poor but pagan poor as well, and urging pagan priests to build hostels and distribute grain to compete. In Cappadocia Basil of Caesarea founded a large complex around 370 to house and treat the poor, the sick, and travelers, often called the Basileias, and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus preached an oration on love for the poor. In the late fourth century John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch on the rich man and Lazarus, argued that failing to share one's goods with the poor amounts to robbing them, and Ambrose of Milan made a similar case in his treatise On Naboth. The Rule of Benedict (sixth century) told monks to receive every guest as Christ, with special care for the poor and pilgrims, on the strength of Matthew 25. Thomas Aquinas taught in the Summa Theologiae (II-II, question 66, article 7) that what a person has in superabundance is owed by natural law to the relief of the poor, and that in urgent, manifest need taking what is necessary to survive is not properly theft.

The Reformation reorganized poor relief rather than abandoning it. In 1523 the Saxon town of Leisnig set up a common chest, administered by elected members of the parish, for the poor, the sick, and schooling, and Luther published its ordinance with his own preface as a model for other towns. Calvin's Ecclesiastical Ordinances for Geneva (1541) gave deacons the care of the poor and the hospital as a standing office of the church. Across the following centuries these convictions fed the work of Christians in hospitals, orphanages, and movements against slavery; the evangelical campaign led in Parliament by William Wilberforce won the abolition of the British slave trade in 1807. As industrial cities grew, Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum Novarum (1891) defended the rights of workers to a just wage and to form associations, and Abraham Kuyper opened the first Christian Social Congress in Amsterdam in November 1891 with an address later published in English as The Problem of Poverty. Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno (1931) set out the principle of subsidiarity, that larger bodies such as the state should not take over what families and smaller communities can do, while helping them do it.

The twentieth century sharpened the debate. The Latin American bishops meeting at Medellín (1968) and Gustavo Gutiérrez in A Theology of Liberation (1971) called the church to stand with the poor against unjust structures, and the bishops at Puebla (1979) spoke of a preferential option for the poor, a phrase later taken up in papal teaching. Evangelicals issued the Chicago Declaration of Evangelical Social Concern (1973), and the Lausanne Covenant (1974), section 5, confessed penitence for having treated evangelism and social concern as mutually exclusive and affirmed that both belong to Christian duty, while section 6 said that in the church's mission of sacrificial service evangelism is primary. Latin American evangelicals such as René Padilla and Samuel Escobar pressed at Lausanne for what came to be called integral mission. In the United States, John Perkins helped found the Christian Community Development Association (1989) to rebuild poor neighborhoods from within. These documents and movements disagree on much, but they share a conviction that runs back through Leisnig and Basil to Deuteronomy: the church cannot confess the God who defends the widow and the stranger and leave them undefended.

differ.view: Evangelism first, with mercy as its fruit
differ.body: Many evangelical and Reformed Christians hold that the church's distinctive mission is to proclaim the gospel, make disciples, and gather them into churches (Matthew 28:18-20), and that deeds of mercy flow from that mission as its necessary fruit and as the duty of every Christian as a neighbor. They note that the New Testament's organized relief was directed chiefly to believers (Acts 6; Romans 15:26; Galatians 6:10), and they warn that when social work becomes the church's main task, the one message no one else will bring is quietly lost. Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert argue this in What Is the Mission of the Church? (2011), and the Lausanne Covenant's statement that evangelism is primary is often cited. Defenders insist this is not indifference to the poor but clarity about what only the church can do.

Others, especially from the Majority World, argue that word and deed are two sides of one mission and should not be ranked. René Padilla and Samuel Escobar pressed this at Lausanne in 1974, and the Micah Network's declaration on integral mission (2001) set it out. They point to Jesus' own ministry, which joined preaching with healing and feeding (Matthew 4:23; Luke 4:18), to the prophets' insistence that worship without justice is rejected, and to James's teaching that faith without works is dead. On this view the church's care for the poor is itself a witness to the kingdom, and a gospel preached without it is not heard as good news. Defenders affirm that people need to be reconciled to God and hold that proclamation keeps its central place within a single, undivided calling.

differ.view: The preferential option for the poor
differ.body: Liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez, and in a moderated form Catholic social teaching after Puebla (1979), hold that God shows a particular concern for the poor throughout Scripture, from the exodus to the Magnificat, and that the church must share it by standing with the poor and reading its own situation from their side. They stress that poverty is often produced by unjust structures (Isaiah 10:1-2; Amos 2:6-7), so that charity alone is not enough; the prophets called for justice in law and courts. Defenders say this does not mean God loves the poor more or that poverty saves, but that a church which does not see the world through the eyes of the poor has not yet read the Bible it holds.

Christians shaped by Catholic teaching on subsidiarity and by Abraham Kuyper's teaching on the distinct spheres of family, church, and state agree that God requires justice for the poor but differ with others on who should carry it out. They argue that the Bible places the primary duty on families (1 Timothy 5:4, 8), congregations, neighbors, and voluntary generosity, that the law of Israel was given to a covenant nation rather than as a blueprint for modern welfare states, and that distant bureaucracies can weaken the relationships through which poverty is best relieved. Defenders affirm that governments must judge fairly and restrain oppression (Romans 13:3-4; Psalm 82) and hold that the question is how, not whether, a society cares for its weakest members.

errors:
The church has refused to spiritualize the poor out of the Bible. Reading ‘the poor’ only as a symbol of spiritual need runs against the gleaning laws, the prophets' charges, Jesus' banquet guests, and Paul's collection, all of which concern real hunger, debt, and wages. It has also refused the opposite error, that poverty is itself righteousness or that the poor are saved by being poor; the law forbids favoring the poor in court (Leviticus 19:15), and the New Testament calls rich and poor alike to repentance and faith. Using Jesus' saying that the poor will always be with us as an excuse for doing nothing reverses the meaning of the Deuteronomy text he was echoing. And the teaching that poverty always signals God's disfavor, while wealth proves his blessing, is answered by Job, by the Psalms of the righteous sufferer, and by the poverty of Jesus himself.

Other distortions are quieter. One is charity that keeps the giver in control and the receiver in shame, which Jesus rejected when he told his followers to give in secret (Matthew 6:2-4) and James condemned in the church that seated the rich man first. Another is the conviction that God cares about the stranger in general but not the particular foreigner next door, which the law answers by grounding love of the stranger in Israel's own memory of being strangers. A third is setting worship against justice, as if either could stand alone. The prophets rejected sacrifice without justice, and the New Testament rejects justice cut loose from the gospel of the God who raised Jesus.
life:
This doctrine reaches into ordinary decisions: what an employer pays and when, whether a landlord keeps a vulnerable tenant's deposit, whom a family invites to dinner, how a congregation spends its budget, and how a Christian votes and speaks about immigrants, prisoners, and the unemployed. Scripture does not settle every policy question, and Christians of good faith reach different conclusions. It does settle the direction of the heart. God's people are to know the names of the widow, the orphan, the poor, and the stranger near them, and to treat their cause as God's own, because the law says he hears their cry and Jesus says he is found among them.

It also shapes prayer and hope. The Psalms give the afflicted words to cry to God and give the comfortable words of repentance. The memory the law kept alive, ‘you were strangers in Egypt’, becomes for Christians the memory that they were once far off and were brought near by the one who became poor for them. That memory makes generosity a form of gratitude rather than pride, and it keeps the church looking toward the day when no one will hunger again.
questions: Israel's law repeatedly grounds care for the foreigner in the memory of slavery in Egypt. What memory of your own, or of the gospel, does that motive call up for you?

Luke's Gospel has “Blessed are you who are poor” and Matthew's has “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” How do the two forms together guard against reading the poor out of the Bible or reading God out of poverty?

The positions described here agree that God requires justice for the poor but differ on whose task it is and how it should be done. Where does your congregation's practice fall, and what would the prophets or James ask of it?
